definition: Very rich, costly, or generous, often more than is strictly needed.
example: The old hotel lobby was lavish, with crystal chandeliers and marble floors.
nuance: Lavish stresses rich abundance and generosity; extravagant more strongly suggests spending beyond what is sensible.
prompt: A family hosts a large wedding reception for their daughter.
options: The reception featured a lavish buffet with six kinds of dessert.
The lavish meal was one bowl of plain rice for every three guests.
The napkins were folded and dyed a soft lavish shade of light purple.
Everyone agreed the party felt lavish because the speeches ended on schedule.
reasons: A huge, costly spread of food for guests shows rich abundance.
Scarce, simple food is the opposite of rich plenty.
This confuses the word with lavender; it does not name a color.
Punctual speeches have nothing to do with richness or expense.

practice.prompt: A soccer coach speaks to the team after a hard-fought win.
options: The coach handed out lavish instructions, timed down to the exact second.
After the long bus ride home, the tired team felt lavish and fell asleep.
She gave lavish praise to every player, even the substitutes.
His idea of lavish praise was muttering "fine" and walking off the field.
reasons: This mistakes the word for precise; it means plentiful, not exact.
The word describes rich abundance, not a feeling of weariness.
Generous, abundant compliments for everyone fit the word well.
A single grudging word is stingy, not generous or abundant.
